# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules

This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).

The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
prose below).

## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate

- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
  never a direct commit to its `main`.
- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
  conversation-extract prune is skipped rather than failing).

## Canon-specific gotchas

- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
  that catches it.
- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
  exception: it commits a whole working tree under the member's delivery preference.)
- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
- **`subscribe_pr_activity` blocks for minutes — subscribe once, and never as a way to "wait for
  CI".** It reads like a cheap registration, so a session calls it, gets no answer, and calls it
  again on the same PR. Measured in the #520 session (`2026-07-28T2208Z`): two consecutive calls on
  PR #524 cost **237s + 220s**, and a `send_later` check-in a further **101s** — **558s of that
  session's 841s of total tool wall-clock (66%)**, all pure idle, in a session whose actual work was
  153 tool calls. One subscription per PR is all there is to gain; a second adds nothing but the
  wait. When what you actually want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge
  on the already-green result — don't buy the same notification twice.
- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
  the repo root.

This is a new rule from GCEC about converting prose to checks. Can you apply this rule (add to the skill) and also run it on all existing checks, to see if some prose can be eliminated?

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

name: prose-to-checks
description: Mine a repo's existing pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or when the growth prose-to-checks sweep runs.
---

# Convert existing prose to checks

A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs. The growth *extract* stage converts each **new**
lesson down the promotion ladder; this pass sweeps the **existing** prose backlog for rules that
are always-testable but still live only as prose — and converts them, so the packs keep shedding
context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is first learned. It runs as
grow_with_claudinite's daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` task, and on demand.

## Scope — the pack paths you were given

Work only the **pack paths configured for this repo** (the task passes them in its Context): a
consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.

## What to look for — the check-the-world test

For each rule, ask the one question from
[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**

- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

## How to convert one

Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:

1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
   doesn't ship.
3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
   directional by kind.
4. **Trim the prose** to rationale — the check owns enforcement now; leaving both pays twice and
   springs the drift trap.

**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — trimming prose is only for a rule a *landed* check
  now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before opening the PR; open it for the owner's approval,
  never a direct push to `main`.

# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose

Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).

## The method lives in the skill

The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.

## What a run does

1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".

## What this task must never do

- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.

1	# Checks — deterministic enforcement of the corpus (design)
2	
3	> **Status: implemented** (issue #127, #131). The runner, the baseline + technology packs, Stop
4	> hook, PreToolUse guard, and the pack-prose loader are live; the corpus is reorganized into
5	> `packs/` (prose + checks, active by declaration) and `skills/` (activity-scoped procedures).
6	> This doc is the rationale and the ongoing design record. The per-rule audit lives in
7	> [docs/conversion-inventory.md](../../docs/conversion-inventory.md).
8	
9	## The problem
10	
11	The corpus enforces style/practice rules as instructions. Instructions have three standing costs:
12	
13	1. **Context** — the always-on baseline loads every session whether or not it's needed, and
14	   adherence degrades as loaded context grows.
15	2. **Silent trigger failure** — soft-loaded docs depend on the agent following their trigger
16	   ("read filePlacement.md before placing a file"), which is itself instruction-following that
17	   fails silently. A rule the agent didn't read can't help.
18	3. **Invisible obsolescence** — a rule a newer Claude Code follows by default keeps costing
19	   tokens and attention forever; nothing measures that it stopped earning its place.
20	
21	A deterministic check inverts all three: it costs zero context until violated, fires whether or
22	not anything was read, and its firing history is measurable — a check that never fails is
23	evidence its rule can retire.
24	
25	## Why this is the right mechanism
26	
27	Anthropic's published guidance says this directly: hooks exist to provide "deterministic control
28	… ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them"
29	(hooks guide); CLAUDE.md is "context, not enforced" (memory doc); and the core best-practice is
30	"give Claude a check it can run … Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and
31	iterates until the check passes" (best practices). The corpus already states the principle in
32	an agent-practices skill: *"Prose is a request; the
33	post-hoc diff check is the guarantee."* This design scales that sentence up.
34	
35	## What converts — and what doesn't
36	
37	An instruction leaves context only when a deterministic mechanism can carry it. Four targets,
38	picked per rule:
39	
40	| Mechanism | Fits when | Examples from the corpus |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **Post-hoc check** (this system) | The rule constrains the *state of the repo* after work | file placement, dangling references, workflow lint, lifecycle compliance |
43	| **PreToolUse hook** | The action must be blocked *before* it runs | never delete a remote branch; don't `issue_write`-overwrite an issue body |
44	| **Skill / script** | A *procedure* or *knowledge* with a nameable (or path-scoped) trigger | the merge recipe; the lessons pass; the technology gotcha files |
45	| **Platform setting** | The platform enforces it outright, for free | squash-only merges; branch protection |
46	
47	Two classes deliberately **stay as instructions**:
48	
49	- **Process/judgment rules** — problem-first consensus, bug investigation method, naming
50	  quality. They shape work *in flight* and leave no artifact a check can inspect. Converting
51	  them post-hoc would also catch violations only after the expensive rework they exist to
52	  prevent.
53	- **Platform-gotcha knowledge** (`technologies/`) — split **per gotcha**, by whether the bad
54	  pattern has a *static signature in the artifact*. Where it does, it converts to a tech-pack
55	  check — a SAM `Handler` still carrying the entry's subdirectory under an esbuild build, an
56	  esbuild declared in `devDependencies`, a `SetIcon({path: …})`, a CloudFront custom
57	  origin-request policy listing `Authorization` — and the agent never needs to know the gotcha
58	  in advance: writing the bad pattern fails the check in the same session, moving discovery
59	  from runtime (often the first deploy or invoke) to write-time, with the gotcha's teaching in
60	  the failure message. Only the signature-less residue stays as skill knowledge: runtime
61	  divergence invisible in the artifact (jsdom *behaving* unlike Chrome, CORS being decided
62	  server-side) and diagnostic know-how. The release pack's **contract** is the
63	  largest signature-rich case — a conformance suite waiting to be written.
64	
65	## Architecture
66	
67	```
68	packs/                        # the mounted corpus: prose + checks, active by declaration
69	  registry.mjs                #   structural discovery — any packs/<name>/pack.mjs is a pack
70	  load-active-prose.mjs       #   SessionStart hook: emits active packs' RULES.md
71	  <baseline>/                 #   the baseline: RULES.md + the core checks (declared like any pack)
72	  <technology>/               #   coding gotchas (RULES.md, prose only)
73	  <technology>-release/       #   RELEASE.md (standard) + stubs + conformance checks (opt-in)
74	  <technology>/               #   the workflow lints (no prose)
75	  <technology>/  <technology>/  …      # more prose-only tech packs
76	  <project-class>/            #   a project-class pack (prose-only, declared)
77	checks/                       # the ENGINE only (runs the packs' checks)
78	  run.mjs                     #   dependency-free Node CLI
79	  lib/                        #   git diff scoping, findings format, markdown + manifest helpers
80	  stop-hook.mjs               #   blocks the agent's stop on blocking findings
81	  pretooluse-guard.mjs        #   blocks forbidden actions before they run
82	  test/                       #   fixtures (scratch git repos), red-first
83	packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/   # activity-scoped procedures, bundled in their owning pack
84	  checks.mjs                  #   the test-the-world checks that validate this skill's action
85	```
86	
87	**Skill-owned checks.** A skill defines the performance of an *action*; the test-the-world
88	check that validates that action's result belongs **beside the SKILL.md that defines it**, not
89	in a pack that owns none of the context. So a skill may carry its own checks — the
90	`routine-structure` check lives in its owning skill's folder, next to the routine-authoring
91	prose it enforces, with its test co-located too. A skill lives inside its owning pack
92	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/` — #385), so discovery IS the pack registry: any bundled skill's
93	`checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) is gathered onto the pack (`skillChecks`) and
94	runs when the pack is active. The pack gate only says the project opted into the pack — not
95	that this skill's action ever happened in this repo — so a skill check's `run` must still
96	**detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and return `[]` when
97	the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing before it asserts
98	anything). Get that wrong and the check fires false findings on every unrelated repo the corpus
99	is mounted in. Reserve skill checks for the world-state a skill's action leaves behind; a rule
100	with no skill to anchor it stays a baseline check.
101	
102	**Where a check goes — the litmus test.** Classify by what the checked *artifact* is, not by
103	which doc teaches the fix (the `doc` pointer is where you *learn* the remedy — most baseline
104	checks point at a skill, so it is **not** the classifier):
105	
106	- present in ~every repo (markdown links, file layout, the root `CLAUDE.md`, git history, a
107	  branch's issue reference) → a **baseline** check;
108	- present only when a declared **technology** is (a workflow, a SAM template, the release
109	  stubs) → a **technology-pack** check, whose relevance is gated by declaration;
110	- present **only because one skill's discrete action created it** (a routine folder, from
111	  authoring a routine) → a **skill** check.
112	
113	Only the third — *the artifact would not exist had the action never run* — earns a home in the
114	skill. `routine-structure` is the sole current case: a routine folder exists only because
115	someone authored a routine. `squash-merge-history` points at the merge skill but stays
116	in the baseline, because git history exists in every repo and is disturbed by any merge, not only that
117	skill's action; `claude-md-length`, `generated-merge-driver`, and the placement check likewise
118	inspect artifacts every repo has, so they stay in the baseline despite naming a skill in `doc`.
119	
120	**Not every pack-machinery concern is a check.** The `.claudinite-checks.json` *settings* are
121	validated when the file loads, not by a conformance rule: malformed JSON, an unknown property,
122	and an unknown pack name are equally settings errors, surfaced by the runner as blocking `config`
123	findings. A pack's `marker` only *suspects* the pack is wanted — whether to declare it is the
124	project's call — so nothing checks that a declared pack carries its marker, or that a marker's
125	pack is declared. Pack **dependencies** (`requires`) are likewise resolved when the declaration is
126	*written* — bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill run `resolveDeclaredPacks` to pull each
127	declared pack's transitive `requires` into the file, materializing the prerequisite (like
128	the baseline) rather than nagging at every Stop. A materialized dependency is written as
129	`{ "id": ..., "via": [...] }` — `via` naming the declared packs that require it — so the file
130	itself records why the dependency is there.
131	
132	**Runner contract.** `node .claudinite/checks/run.js`. Dependency-free Node — no `npm install`
133	step exists on the tarball mount, and the corpus's own "earn each dependency" rule applies to
134	us first. Exit 0 = clean, exit 1 = blocking findings. The default scope is the **whole repo**:
135	on a text corpus the full sweep costs milliseconds, and only full scope sees cross-file
136	breakage — a change in one file dangling a reference in an unchanged one. The steady state is
137	a repo at zero findings (or reviewed acceptances), held there by every run. `--changed`
138	(diff vs the merge-base with main) exists only as a transitional aid while adopting a repo
139	that carries a backlog — it is not the enforcement default. (Rules that are inherently about
140	the *delta* — new suppression markers, commits referencing an issue — diff against the
141	merge-base in either scope.)
142	
143	**Pack selection: declared for deterministic execution, fingerprinted against drift.** The
144	packs a project runs are **pinned in `.claudinite-checks.json`**
145	(`"packs": ["baseline", "a-technology-pack", "a-release-pack"]`; no pack runs
146	undeclared — the baseline too is declared explicitly, seeded by bootstrap).
147	Execution is a closed, declared set: every rule in a declared pack
148	runs when its scope's surface runs — the work rules at the Stop hook, the world rules in the
149	test/CI flow — with no inference at execution time, so "the
150	project uses technology X" deterministically implies "every X check ran." Bootstrap writes the
151	initial declaration from the repo's fingerprint — a pack's `detect` marker (`.github/workflows/`
152	→ a workflow-lint pack; a `manifest.json` with `manifest_version` → the extension packs; the
153	release-workflow `name:`s → the conformance suite) seeds it at `--init`. But a marker only
154	*suspects* a pack is wanted: from then on the declaration is authoritative, and whether to add a
155	newly adopted technology's pack, or drop one whose technology has left, is the **project's** call
156	— the checker never second-guesses it. What *is* enforced is settings **validity**: an unknown
157	pack name, an unknown property, or malformed JSON is caught when the file loads
158	(`loadConfig` + the runner) and surfaced as a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as
159	much a settings error as bad JSON. `.claudinite-checks.json` additionally holds per-rule
160	**overrides** and **acceptances** — at the top level for project-wide decisions, or on a pack's
161	own entry for the ones that pack's declaration motivates (see engine/checks/README.md).
162	
163	A declared id may name a **canon** pack or one of the repo's **own local packs**
164	(`.claudinite/local_packs/<id>/` — the project's tracked, project-specific packs, discovered from
165	the repo's own tree alongside the mounted canon; canonically declared by the namespaced token
166	`local_packs/<id>`, the bare id accepted while the fleet migrates — see engine/checks/README.md). Both
167	are the same closed-declared-set execution;
168	`knownIds` spans both, so a local id is valid, not an unknown-pack error, while a broken or
169	id-colliding local `pack.mjs` is surfaced as a blocking `config` finding rather than silently
170	dropping the pack's checks. A local pack's checks run when it is declared, exactly like a canon
171	pack's; this is where a project's *own* deterministic rules live (the checks-over-prose economy,
172	applied at the project's level) instead of always-loaded prose.
173	
174	**Acceptances are the escape hatch — deterministic and reviewable.** Rules with judgment
175	exemptions (a placement rule's "deliberate cross-cutting concern") need a way to say "yes, on
176	purpose" that isn't a fight with the hook: a per-finding `accept` entry with a mandatory reason
177	string, keyed by rule id + path. It lands in the diff like any code, so the *decision* gets
178	reviewed once instead of re-litigated every session. An acceptance a pack's adoption forces
179	lives on that pack's `packs` entry, so its provenance — which declaration required which
180	exception — is the file's own structure.
181	
182	An acceptance is a **check-the-world** instrument: a persistent, committed exemption a future
183	sweep keeps re-finding and must be told to ignore. It is the wrong tool for a **check-the-work**
184	finding — a conversation- or branch-scoped rule (e.g. `feature-requirements-first`) whose finding
185	a fresh session wouldn't even re-raise; accepting one leaves a permanent suppression for a
186	one-session artifact. Author a check-the-work rule to be **satisfiable by fixing the work, or to
187	self-skip** when its precondition isn't met (the spec it enforces against isn't in the repo, say):
188	a finding no correct work can clear forces the wrong remedy — an accept, or a post-hoc rebase —
189	so it's a bug in the rule, not a candidate for an acceptance.
190	
191	And when a rule mandates an **ordering** — X must happen before Y — it ships with a
192	check-the-work verification of that order, judged on the surface where the order is visible:
193	the conversation transcript (`feature-requirements-first`'s comment-scoped doc-first ordering)
194	or the branch commit log (a rule-before-fix test asserting the outlawing commit is an ancestor
195	of the fixing one, `pack-independence`'s pattern). A stated ordering with no check-the-work
196	verifier is prose-only enforcement — exactly what this system exists to replace.
197	
198	**The finding is the instruction.** This is the context economy of the whole design: the rule's
199	teaching text moves out of always-loaded context and into the failure message, paying its token
200	cost only on violation, in the session that violated it, pointed at the exact spot. Every
201	finding carries: rule id, `file:line`, what's wrong, *why* (one line — the model generalizes
202	from motivation), the fix, and a doc pointer for depth.
203	
204	<example>
205	
206	```
207	reference-distance  src/report/render.js:12
208	  imports ../../util/dates.js at distance 4.
209	  Why: the folder tree should encode the dependency graph; far reaches make it lie.
210	  Fix: move dates.js next to its users, lift it to a common ancestor, or accept it
211	       in .claudinite-checks.json with a reason if it's a deliberate cross-cutting util.
212	  More: .claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
213	```
214	
215	</example>
216	
217	## Enforcement wiring
218	
219	The two scopes fire at **different times**, because they answer different questions. The *work*
220	scope judges the change in front of the session and belongs on a per-turn hook; the *world* scope
221	is a whole-repo invariant assertion — the same shape as a test suite — and belongs wherever the
222	project runs its tests, not on every turn.
223	
224	**Work scope: a Stop hook is the guarantee; instructions are not.** Bootstrap registers one hook
225	in the consumer's `.claude/settings.json` (the same mechanism as the existing SessionStart hooks):
226	
227	1. The Stop hook fires when the agent finishes a turn.
228	2. It **fast-exits in milliseconds** when no tracked file differs from `main` — conversational
229	   turns cost nothing.
230	3. Otherwise it runs the **work** sweep (`check_the_work.mjs`, with the session transcript); on
231	   findings it exits 2 with them on stderr. Claude Code blocks the stop and feeds that text back
232	   to the agent, which fixes the violations **in the same session**. A clean run stops silently.
233	
234	Loop safety comes from convergence (fixed findings stop firing) plus Claude Code's own runaway
235	protection (it overrides a Stop hook after ~8 consecutive blocks).
236	
237	**World scope: wired into the project's test/CI flow (revises #385).** The whole-repo sweep runs
238	as its own step wherever the project runs its tests — a CI job, a `make test` target, an npm
239	script — invoked as the standalone `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`
240	command. It is deliberately **not** a language-specific test file (a `*.test.mjs` a Node runner
241	discovers): a Python/Rust/Go consumer's suite could not load one, and the sweep is the engine's
242	own always-vendored Node CLI, so it runs as a step in any flow regardless of the project's
243	language. Bootstrap wires this step during adoption, adding a minimal flow where the repo has
244	none. This **supersedes the original #385 decision** ("the Stop hook is the whole enforcement
245	surface; consumers ship no CI job"): the earlier design kept the world sweep on Stop to spare
246	consumers a CI setup, but running a whole-repo sweep every turn is work misplaced in time, and a
247	human editing on GitHub web (or any non-session tool) is now caught by the test/CI flow the
248	change lands through rather than by the next session's Stop.
249	
250	**The conversation surface (Stop hook only).** Some process rules leave their artifact not in
251	the repo but in the *session itself* — e.g. `comment-classification` (the reply to the owner's
252	latest comment must declare an explicit `Comment class:` line: the assessment stays judgment,
253	but that an assessment was made is checkable) and `feature-requirements-first` (a
254	feature-classified comment's doc-first ordering on the branch). The Stop hook is the one surface
255	that can carry these: Claude Code passes the hook `transcript_path` on stdin, the hook forwards
256	it as `--transcript`, and `ctx.conversation()` exposes the parsed session
257	([helpers/session-transcript.mjs](helpers/session-transcript.mjs)). Everywhere else — CI, a manual run — the transcript
258	is absent and these rules self-gate to `[]`, the same self-supplied relevance gate skill checks
259	use. Two scoping choices keep them convergent rather than nagging: only the *latest* owner
260	comment is judged (a transcript is append-only, so an old omission could never be fixed), and
261	the ordering rule scopes to commits after the comment's timestamp (earlier work on the branch is
262	never re-litigated). The Stop hook's clean fast path also means a purely conversational turn —
263	no tracked change vs the base — runs no checks at all, conversation rules included.
264	
265	**Prefer a platform setting when one exists — but never trust it.** Squash-only merging is a
266	GitHub repo setting; force-push protection is branch protection. The setting does the
267	*enforcing*, but it's configuration like any other: it can be off, get switched off, or be
268	bypassed, and nothing notices. So every setting rung pairs with a check that verifies it, in
269	order of strength:
270	
271	- **Effect check (preferred)** — offline and deterministic, it verifies the *outcome* the
272	  setting guarantees rather than the setting itself: squash-only ⇒ the change lands squashed,
273	  so its own commits carry no merge commit (`squash-merge-history` in the baseline pack). It
274	  is scoped to the work — the merge commits the current change introduces on HEAD's first-parent
275	  chain since the merge-base — not the repo's whole history: it catches the setting being off or
276	  bypassed *for this change* without re-auditing (and demanding acceptances for) legacy merges
277	  already on `main` that the work never touched. Testing the work, not the world, is what keeps
278	  the check from firing on every unrelated session.
279	
280	  **A work-scoped rule is only as honest as the ref it scopes against.** "Since the merge-base"
281	  is a correct definition that silently becomes a wrong verdict when the base ref is stale —
282	  a cloud session's clone freezes `origin/main` at container-creation time, so everything the
283	  base branch gained since then reads as introduced by the work, and a *blocking* rule starts
284	  reporting other people's merges on a branch that has none of its own. Two mechanisms keep the
285	  scope honest, both in `buildContext` rather than in any one rule: the base ref is refreshed
286	  before the merge-base is computed (best-effort, bounded, opt-out — [README](README.md)), and
287	  candidates are confirmed against the base ref itself, because `git merge-base` returns one of
288	  several equally-good answers on a criss-cross history and the one it picks can leave a merge
289	  that is already on the base branch inside the range. Scoping a delta rule is two jobs: pick
290	  the range, and make sure the range's endpoint is telling the truth.
291	- **Config check** — reads the setting via the platform API and fails when it's off. Needs a
292	  network-capable surface: rules carry a surface tag, the Stop hook runs only offline rules,
293	  CI runs what its repo token can read (e.g. the allow-merge-commit flags), and the fleet
294	  maintenance routine covers settings a repo token can't (e.g. branch protection). Follow-up
295	  work alongside the Phase 2 packs.
296	
297	## Governance
298	
299	- **A converted rule leaves its doc.** The check's failure message owns the rule now; the doc
300	  keeps only rationale and the judgment parts. Keeping both pays twice and springs the corpus's
301	  own drift trap (two sources of truth).
302	- **Fail fast: a new check ships at its real severity — blocking for defect-kind rules.** A
303	  wrong blocking check surfaces in the very next session and gets fixed; an advisory false
304	  positive is noise nobody reads, so a burn-in stage never actually observes the precision it
305	  waits for. The escape hatches bound a bad check's blast radius: a reasoned acceptance, a
306	  severity override, and the Stop hook's own two-block release. `advisory` remains a per-rule
307	  **kind**, not a stage — for rules whose own semantics are directional (a placement rule's
308	  metric is "a direction, not a hard gate"), where a finding is a smell to judge, not a defect
309	  to fix. Revisit delayed adoption only if the fleet grows people who can be hurt by a wrong
310	  block.
311	- **Telemetry drives retirement.** The runner logs firings; the fleet-maintenance routine
312	  already reads every vendored repo and can report "rules that never fired in N days" —
313	  obsolescence made measurable, the property instructions never had.
314	
315	## Skills — the on-demand layer for what checks can't carry
316	
317	Checks carry the *enforceable* rules. Everything else that today rides on soft pointers —
318	procedures, task-gated practices, technology knowledge — moves to **Agent Skills**, a mechanism
319	the system doesn't use yet. The docs' own decision rule fits exactly: *"Create a skill when …
320	a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact"*, and knowledge-bearing
321	skills are explicitly endorsed (*"reference content adds knowledge … conventions, patterns,
322	style guides, domain knowledge"*). The official hook-vs-skill line mirrors this design's ladder:
323	*"Use a hook when the action must happen the same way every time … Use a skill when Claude
324	should decide how to apply the steps, or when the content is knowledge rather than a script."*
325	
326	**What a skill buys over a CLAUDE.md soft pointer.** The token economics are roughly neutral —
327	a skill's name + description sit in context every session (progressive disclosure: the body
328	loads only on invocation), about what an index line costs today. The real gain is **trigger
329	reliability**: today a `tasks/` doc helps only if the agent remembers to follow the index line
330	("read before writing a test") — an instruction-following step that fails silently. Skill
331	matching is harness-managed and trained-for, skills are user-invocable as `/name` too (manual
332	invocation is deterministic — it runs when typed), and technology skills can be
333	**`paths`-scoped** (glob frontmatter) so they surface exactly when the matching files are
334	touched — a structural trigger, not a remembered one.
335	
336	Be clear about what this is *not*: **model-invocation of a skill is still probabilistic** —
337	better odds than a soft pointer, never a guarantee. That is precisely why this design's
338	division of labor puts nothing that *must* happen on a skill: enforcement lives in hooks,
339	checks, and settings, which are deterministic by construction; skills carry only guidance whose
340	worst-case miss is today's status quo. In particular, check execution never depends on skill
341	routing — the Stop hook runs the declared packs whether or not any skill fired. The split is
342	therefore **per-rule, not per-doc**: a doc's enforceable rules go to a pack (which runs
343	unconditionally for every project that declares it), its judgment residue rides the skill, and
344	there is deliberately no one-to-one correspondence between an instruction file and a pack. Two documented limits
345	to respect: keep descriptions tight (the listing truncates them, and the description budget
346	scales with the context window — many verbose skills degrade matching), and keep each
347	`SKILL.md` body well under 500 lines.
348	
349	### The catalog
350	
351	There is no skill catalog (#385): a skill is its owning pack's content
352	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the pack's own README names what it bundles, and the
353	harness surfaces skills by their frontmatter descriptions, which is the routing.
354	
355	What stays always-loaded after this: a trimmed
356	baseline `RULES.md`, the judgment core of
357	the agent-practices skill (its trigger — "writing
358	code" — is near-universal, so a skill gains little; revisit with telemetry), and a much smaller
359	index. The routing index largely dissolves: routing *is what skill descriptions do natively*.
360	
361	### Delivery — incremental now, plugin end-state
362	
363	- **Now (works with both mount methods):** each skill is bundled in its owning pack
364	  (`<pack>/skills/<name>/`), and the SessionStart hook `engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`
365	  regenerates `.claude/skills/<name>` symlinks for the active packs' union each session —
366	  nothing committed (a committed link dangles on every plain checkout). Symlinked skill
367	  directories are documented, supported behavior, and skill changes are picked up live within
368	  a session — so mounts generated at session start still land, the same property the tarball
369	  sync populating their targets already relies on.
370	- **Later, maybe — Claudinite as a plugin (contingent on a spike).** A plugin is nothing
371	  exotic: a directory layout inside an ordinary git repo (`skills/`, `commands/`,
372	  `hooks/hooks.json`, a `plugin.json` manifest) plus a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` that
373	  lets the repo serve as its own catalog. **No publication to Anthropic** — any git repo works
374	  as a marketplace directly, and the repo may carry arbitrary other content alongside the
375	  plugin dirs, so Claudinite would remain exactly the freely-amended GitHub repo it is (growth
376	  PRs, this doc, everything — unchanged). The draw: plugins bundle precisely this design's
377	  pieces — skills, commands, and hooks (SessionStart, Stop, PreToolUse) with bundled scripts
378	  addressable via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — and a consumer repo can commit
379	  `extraKnownMarketplaces` + `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json` to enable it for
380	  everyone. **Why it is not the plan of record:** the docs leave the operational questions that
381	  matter most to this system unanswered — how promptly consumers receive updates (manual
382	  `/plugin marketplace update` is documented; session-start auto-refresh is not), whether
383	  web/cloud sessions load marketplace plugins at all, and whether plugin hooks behave
384	  identically to settings-registered ones. A daily-growth corpus lives or dies on update
385	  latency, and the current SessionStart tarball sync *guarantees* latest-`main` every session.
386	  So: phases 1–4 ship entirely on the existing mount + symlinks and depend on the plugin route
387	  for nothing; adopt it only if a Phase-5 spike proves same-day propagation, web support, and
388	  hook parity. (Also documented: a plugin cannot inject always-on CLAUDE.md-style prose, so the
389	  residual baseline keeps its `@`-import either way.)
390	
391	## Growth pipeline: checks-first promotion
392	
393	New lessons enter the canon through the growth lifecycle (extract → promote → dedup). Today
394	the promote step generalizes a lesson and routes it to a prose doc.
395	Under this design, **prose becomes the fallback, not the default** — the point of promotion is
396	to relieve every project's context, and a check relieves it completely while prose only
397	relocates it.
398	
399	**The promotion ladder.** Every lesson that clears the worthiness bar is triaged down the same
400	mechanism order as the conversion table above — the *first* rung that can carry it wins:
401	
402	1. **Platform setting** — the platform enforces it outright, always paired with the check
403	   that verifies it holds (effect check first, config check where a token can read it).
404	2. **PreToolUse hook** — a bad action to block before it runs.
405	3. **Post-hoc check** — a constraint on repo state.
406	4. **Skill** — a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger.
407	5. **Prose canon** — only for what none of the above can carry, and the landing **names its
408	   reason** (judgment / in-flight behavior / platform knowledge), logged per lesson in the
409	   promote tracking issue so conversion rates are auditable.
410	
411	Concretely, three growth docs change:
412	
413	- **`item-routing.md`** gains a step 0: *mechanism triage*
414	  before file routing. "Which doc owns this" is only asked for lessons that fall through to
415	  rung 5.
416	- **the promote task doc**: for a rung-3 lesson, the routine authors
417	  the check in the same PR — rule id, detection, the failure message (which *is* the
418	  generalized lesson text), **plus a fixture proving it fires** on a violating input and stays
419	  quiet on a clean one (see-it-fail applies to checks too). When it can't produce a confident
420	  detection + fixture, it lands the lesson as prose **and** opens a tagged conversion-backlog
421	  issue — a visible miss to sweep later, never a silently-shipped broken check.
422	- **the dedup task doc**: a canon **check** covers a local prose item the
423	  same way a canon line does — better, since the coverage is enforced rather than stated. The
424	  runner exposes the rule catalog machine-readably (`run.js --list`: rule id, description,
425	  failure message, doc pointer); dedup quotes a **rule id** where it today quotes a canon line.
426	  This answers the obvious worry — "the canon won't have the instruction, only a test": the
427	  check *carries* its instruction as data (its failure message), so dedup compares against the
428	  catalog exactly as it compares against prose today, and more mechanically, since rule ids are
429	  stable where prose wording drifts. The keep-test is unchanged: a local item that says *more*
430	  than the check detects (a stronger point about a narrower case) stays.
431	
432	Extract is untouched: project-local capture stays prose at the project's own level —
433	conversion is a promotion-time judgment, made once, centrally.
434	
435	## Phasing
436	
437	1. **Runner + Stop hook + first baseline checks** — reference-integrity, task-lifecycle,
438	   warning-suppression (blocking); the placement check (advisory by kind). Bootstrap gains the
439	   hook-registration step.
440	2. **a workflow-lint pack + a release-conformance pack**, piloted on one
441	   extension repo.
442	3. **Baseline restructure** — the first skills (a merge recipe, a lessons pass) + the
443	   squash-only setting; temporary-workarounds → PreToolUse hook; slim the converted docs and
444	   the index.
445	4. **Skills layer + growth pivot** — the rest of the corpus (practice + technology skills,
446	   symlink delivery in bootstrap), and the promotion ladder lands in
447	   the promote task doc,
448	   `item-routing.md`, and
449	   the dedup task doc.
450	5. **(Contingent) plugin packaging** — only after a spike proves same-day update propagation,
451	   web-session support, and hook parity; until then the mount + symlink delivery is the plan of
452	   record and nothing depends on this phase.
453	6. **(Deferred)** LLM-judge checks in CI for judgment rules (naming, comment quality) —
454	   possible, but nondeterministic and token-costly; revisit only after 1–4 prove out.
455
